answers.text:
Transfer entropy is a specific information-theoretic measure, distinct from the more familiar mutual information, that's designed to capture directional influence between two signals over time. Where mutual information just tells you how much two neurons' activity patterns overlap or correlate, transfer entropy asks a more targeted question: how much does knowing a source neuron's past activity help predict a target neuron's future activity, above and beyond what you'd already know just from the target's own past (its autocorrelation)?

The article defines this precisely a few sentences later: Transfer entropy is well suited to measuring how much the past activity of one neuron accounts for the immediate future activity of another neuron, conditioned on Y's own past. TE is understood as quantifying how much the past of the source variable reduces our uncertainty about the future of the target variable, after accounting for information disclosed by the target variable's own past. This conditioning on the target's own history is what gives the measure its directional, time-ordered character — it's built to look like genuine "flow" from one neuron to another, rather than just simultaneous co-variation.

The article draws a sharp contrast with mutual information here: Whereas mutual information is a measure of functional connectivity, transfer entropy measures effective connectivity. In practice this means mutual information tells you two neurons are statistically related, while transfer entropy tells you information seems to be propagating from one to the other in a particular direction.

In the structure of the article, this is one of the two foundational tools introduced in this section (alongside mutual information) before the paper moves on to its main subject — partial information decomposition (PID). Transfer entropy matters later because it's the tool the authors' own empirical work uses to first map out which neurons are meaningfully connected (building the "effective network") before PID is applied to ask the deeper question of how those connected neurons jointly process, rather than merely transmit, information.

answers.asked: Information-theoretic tools such as mutual information [10] and transfer entropy [11] are well suited to this purpose.
answers.text:
This sentence is naming the two specific measurement tools the paper is about to unpack, and telling you what each one is good for: tracking how information moves across a neural system, given one neuron (or region) treated as a source and another as a target receiving from it. It's a signpost sentence — the two paragraphs right after this one (in the article) each take one of these tools in turn and give its formal definition.

The distinction the article draws between the two tools is worth having in mind going in, since it comes up again and again later in the paper. As the article explains just afterward, mutual information measures how our ability to correctly infer the state of X changes, depending on whether we are accounting for (potentially) shared dependencies with Y, but it does not, however, quantify information transfer between the neurons, as it is an undirected measure that describes the instantaneous dependency between two variables and has no notion of the time-directed structure that we intuitively understand as "transfer" or "flow." Transfer entropy is the fix for that: it is well suited to measuring how much the past activity of one neuron... accounts for the immediate future activity of another neuron... conditioned on Y's own past. In short, mutual information tells you two neurons' activity is statistically linked; transfer entropy tells you the direction that link runs in, source-to-target.

Both are cited to foundational information-theory papers ([10] and [11] in the reference list) rather than being the authors' own work — they're the established building blocks the paper will later combine into the more elaborate "partial information decomposition" framework that is the real subject of the review.

answers.asked: What does "transfer entropy" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
Transfer entropy is defined in the article as a measure of how much the past activity of one neuron reduces uncertainty about the future activity of another neuron, over and above what that second neuron's own past already tells you. Formally, it's the transfer entropy from a source X's past to a target Y's future, conditioned on Y's own past — so it strips out simple autocorrelation and isolates what the source specifically contributes [spya-p4pyuy]. The article makes a point of contrasting it with mutual information: mutual information is undirected and just measures shared dependency between two variables with no sense of time or "flow," whereas transfer entropy is directional and is described as measuring effective connectivity rather than mere functional connectivity — in short, it is a measure of information propagation between neurons [spya-p4pyuy spya-f6sbgx].

Why it matters to the argument: the piece uses transfer entropy first to build simple directed networks of "who is talking to whom" in a circuit — it's how the authors identify which pairs of source neurons feed into a common target neuron, the triads that all the later partial information decomposition (PID) analysis runs on [spya-qjdbvj spya-sw5ukx]. But the article is explicit that transfer entropy alone can't do the job the paper cares about: it captures the overall flow of information but is limited in its ability to reveal how different streams of information interact or how a neuron produces novel information from combining multiple inputs, i.e., it can't detect synergy [spya-s0db2g spya-wer4cd]. That gap is exactly the motivation for introducing PID, so transfer entropy functions in the argument as the tool that gets you as far as "information moves from X to Y" — and PID is presented as picking up where it stops, decomposing that movement into redundant, unique, and synergistic components [spya-wer4cd spya-u5ra3d]. Later, transfer entropy also reappears as an empirical variable in its own right: the authors report that synergy in a triad tracks the amount of transfer entropy flowing into it, running at roughly a quarter of that value [spya-kqkb58].

In this abstract, "synergistic" describes one of three modes by which a group of neurons carries information about a target — the mode where multiple inputs together reveal something that none of them reveals on its own. The article says PID reveals redundant, unique, and synergistic modes by which neurons integrate information from multiple sources, and singles out synergy as the interesting one because it quantifies the "higher-order" information carried in the patterns of multiple inputs and is not reducible to input from any single source.

Concretely (as the article works out later, in blocks 27–28), if you measure how much two source neurons jointly tell you about a target neuron's future firing, that joint information is not simply the sum of what each neuron tells you individually. When the whole exceeds the sum of the parts, the excess is synergy: information that only shows up when you look at the two sources' activity patterns together, as a combination, rather than one at a time. The article treats this as the signature of actual "computation" or "information processing" happening at the target neuron — the target is doing something more than passively adding up independent signals; it is sensitive to the joint pattern of its inputs. This is why the abstract flags synergy as the mode the review will focus on: it's presented as the clearest information-theoretic fingerprint of neurons integrating, rather than merely relaying, information from upstream sources.

answers.asked: PID reveals redundant, unique, and synergistic modes by which neurons integrate information from multiple sources.
answers.text:
This sentence is naming the three outputs of the framework the abstract just introduced, partial information decomposition (PID), and it's worth unpacking what each of the three words is doing, since the rest of the paper builds entirely on this vocabulary.

The setup is: a target neuron gets input from two or more source neurons, and you want to know how much those sources together tell you about what the target does next. The naive approach would be to just add up how informative each source is on its own — but that total doesn't have to match the informativeness of the sources taken jointly. PID is the method for splitting that joint information into non-overlapping pieces that explain why it doesn't just add up.

Redundant information is what multiple sources tell you that overlaps — knowing either one source or another would already give you this piece, so it isn't gained twice, it's shared. Unique information is what only one particular source can tell you, information no other source has access to. Synergistic information is the interesting one for this review: information that only shows up when you look at the sources jointly, in combination — neither source alone discloses it, but their joint pattern does. The article treats synergy as a signature of actual "computation" or "integration" happening at the target neuron, since it can't be attributed to any single input acting alone.

The article itself explains this trio more fully a few paragraphs later using the two-source case and a Venn-diagram figure, but this sentence in the abstract is essentially previewing that machinery in one line, flagging that PID's payoff is being able to say, for any neuron's inputs, how much of what they jointly reveal is duplicated, how much is exclusive to one source, and how much only emerges from their combination.

answers.asked: What does "synergistic" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
"Synergistic" here means the piece of information about a target neuron's future that can *only* be learned by looking at two (or more) source neurons *together* — it disappears if you look at either source alone. The article defines it in the two-neuron case as `Syn(X1, X2;Y)`, part of the decomposition of the joint mutual information into redundant, unique, and synergistic terms [spya-h5jzvm]. It's illustrated in Figure 1 as the "purple space" that is left over once you subtract what each source individually tells you about the target from the total joint information [spya-pjdgu6].

Why it matters to the argument: the whole paper is built on the idea that synergy is the *signature of computation*, not just signal-passing. The authors state plainly that when the joint information from all inputs exceeds the sum of what each gives alone, "the target neuron can be thought of as performing a kind of integrating 'computation' on all of its inputs considered jointly" — this synergistic excess is what they treat as information *processing* rather than mere information *transfer* [spya-e94ury]. Earlier they set up this contrast explicitly: transfer entropy captures the "flow" of information, but "it is limited in its ability to reveal how different streams of information 'interact' and how neurons produce novel or modified information from multiple sources" [spya-s0db2g] — synergy is what fills that gap.

Every empirical section of the paper then uses the amount of synergy in a triad as its dependent variable — the thing that tracks "how much computing" is happening — and finds it varies systematically with network structure (higher in rich-club triads [spya-fud8q3], higher with more recurrent connections [spya-sd9fzd], non-monotonically related to how correlated the source neurons are [spya-hkhpex spya-ybmve2]) and with behavioral state in primates [spya-t8fayf]. In the summary, the authors make the stakes explicit: the existence of synergy shows "neurons do not appear to blindly sum the number of inputs and fire in response to the total... but instead they are also sensitive to the particular patterns of incoming stimuli" [spya-sp50v3]. So synergy is doing the conceptual work of turning "information flow" into "information processing" — it's the quantity that lets the authors claim neurons genuinely *compute* on their inputs rather than just relay them.
